title: cuda kernel optimization notes - FlashAttention + fused ops + paged KV
content:
Overview

Purpose: capture practical notes for CUDA kernel-level optimizations we should evaluate/implement in the serving runtime: focused on FlashAttention integration, operator fusion opportunities (QKV, bias/residual/layernorm fusions), and a paged KV cache design for large-context models. This is an iterative working doc - experimental results and microbenchmarks live in the repo PR above.

Goals / constraints
- Maximize end-to-end throughput (tokens/s) for typical request distributions (mixed short prompts + occasional long-context streaming).
- Respect latency SLOs for low-p99 tail (<= 300ms for small requests) - prefer techniques that reduce critical-path latency.
- Keep memory overhead bounded to support multi-model allocation on Dedicated nodes.
- Make fallback to reference kernels simple when precision/compatibility needed.

1) FlashAttention: integration notes and pitfalls
- Rationale: FlashAttention gives much better memory bandwidth utilization for attention dense layers by computing attention in tiled streaming fashion, avoiding big softmax buffers. For long sequences (>= 512), we see 2-3x speedups on A100/RTX6000 depending on head dim.
- API surface: prefer to wrap FlashAttention as a drop-in attention op that accepts: q, k, v, cu_seqlens / lengths, causal flag, dropout=0 (inference). Keep options to switch between float16/float32 and fused softmax scaling.
- Memory/streams: FlashAttention expects contiguous Q,K,V layout; our runtime currently stores KV in paged stream-friendly layout for paged-KV. Need a small copy/transpose path when the cached KV pages are not contiguous. Copy cost must be amortized by reduced compute time; measure break-even sequence lengths.
- Causal masking: use the FlashAttention variant that supports causal masking without materializing full mask; verify correctness on variable-length batches.
- Mixed precision: prefer fp16 with fp32 accumulation where available. Watch for models (instruction-tuned) that are sensitive to fp16; add per-model flag to disable fused kernel.
- Performance notes: thread-block sizing tuned for (head_dim / 32) granularity. When head dim is 64 or 128, set tile sizes to maximize SM occupancy. Keep small-head path for dim=16/32 as a separate kernel.
- Fallbacks: when FlashAttention cannot be used (odd head dims, unsupported GPU arch), run standard attention kernel. Keep profiler to detect frequent fallbacks.

2) Fused ops (QKV + out projection + bias + residual + partial layernorm)
- Opportunities:
  - Fuse QKV linear (3x GEMM) into a single batched GEMM when weights are stored interleaved; avoids extra memwrite for intermediate Q/K/V.
  - Fuse attention output projection + bias + residual add + RMSNorm/LayerNorm partial into a single kernel when shapes align.
  - Combine GELU or SwiGLU compute into the MLP kernels where possible.
- Tradeoffs:
  - Fusion reduces global memory traffic but increases register pressure and kernel code complexity. Larger fused kernels can reduce concurrency (fewer kernels in flight) but improve latency for single requests.
  - Maintain modular fallback path so that we can disable specific fused kernels per-model or for debugging.
- Implementation notes:
  - QKV fused GEMM: use cuBLASLt/groupedGemm fallback when layout not ideal; otherwise implement a custom fused kernel that consumes input block and writes Q,K,V into tiled output region. Consider prepacking weight tensors in interleaved layout at model-load time to avoid reformatting.
  - Out projection + residual + LN: perform out_proj GEMM -> accumulate into output buffer, then run a single CUDA kernel that applies bias, adds residual, and does the final layernorm (or RMSNorm). Doing layernorm in the same kernel reduces two memory reads/writes.
  - For fp16 accumulation, use tensor-cores where possible, but ensure correctness for layernorm scale/shift precision.

3) Paged KV cache design notes
- Motivation: support very long-context generation and many concurrent requests without forcing full-length KV to reside in GPU DRAM. Move cold KV pages to host pinned memory/NVMe or to device memory spill pools.
- Page granularity: choose page size in tokens (e.g., 128-512 tokens) tuned to model's typical chunking and attention window. Smaller pages reduce wasted transfer but increase metadata and transfer count.
- Layout and metadata:
  - Represent KV cache as a sequence of pages per layer (immutable once written). Each page has metadata: layer_id, head_dim, start_token_idx, length_tokens, resident_location {device, host_pinned, nvme}, last_access_ts.
  - Keep a compact page table in device memory (array of page descriptors) to map request positions to device pointers for fast address translation inside kernels. Page table must be copyable to device before generation step to avoid host/device hops in the inner loop.
- Eviction/placement policy:
  - LRU-like policy across pages with heuristics to pin recent pages for active beams. Pin pages for the top-K hottest requests.
  - Prewarm next pages for streaming decode (prefetch next N pages to device).
  - Async DMA: move pages using CUDA memcpy async on separate streams to overlap transfers with attention compute.
- Kernel-level handling:
  - Attention kernels should accept either a contiguous KV pointer or an indirection vector of per-head/per-page pointers. Indirection hurts performance; prefer staging: for pages that are not resident, copy them into a small device-side staging buffer (per-GPU) and then run a single attention kernel that consumes the staged contiguous block.
  - For extreme concurrency, allow per-request persistent attention kernel that reads from multiple small device buffers to avoid creating too many short-lived kernels.
- Performance caveats:
  - PCIe/NVLink bandwidth is the limiter: prefetching too many pages saturates links and hurts other workloads. Institute adaptive prefetch windows based on observed link utilization.
  - NVMe-as-spill requires careful batching of IO; using GPUDirect Storage where available reduces CPU copy overhead.

4) Scheduling and kernel execution strategies
- Stream/SM utilization:
  - Use multiple CUDA streams: one for compute, one for async transfers, and one low-priority stream for background prefetch/evict work.
  - Bind long-running persistent kernels (for batched attention) to dedicated streams and use cooperative groups where beneficial.
- Kernel fusion vs concurrency:
  - For small-batch low-latency requests, fused kernels that do QKV->attention->outproj in a single kernel reduce scheduling overhead and memory traffic.
  - For large-batch throughput, splitting into multiple smaller kernels that allow concurrent execution can yield better SM utilization. Provide runtime heuristics: if batch_size * seq_len > threshold -> opt for unfused/concurrent path; else fused-latency path.
- Occupancy tuning:
  - Autotune block/thread sizes on first model-inference or at build time for each GPU arch. Store a tiny tuning table per model (head_dim, seq_len ranges) to pick kernel variants.
- Preemption and fairness:
  - Cooperative preemption: break long kernels into smaller tiles to allow SLO-critical requests to preempt. When a high-priority request arrives, cancel or reduce batch size of low-priority jobs and reschedule.

5) Benchmarks and measurement plan
- Microbenchmarks:
  - Single-layer attention: vary head_dim in {32,64,128,256}, seq_len in {32,128,512,2048}, batch in {1,8,64}. Measure tokens/s, latency p50/p95, and GPU memory throughput (GB/s).
  - End-to-end generation: measure tokens/s and p99 latency on typical mixed workloads (50% short prompts < 64 tokens, 50% longer contexts streaming).
  - Paged KV experiments: measure hit/miss rate, transfer bandwidth, end-to-end latency change with varying page sizes and prefetch windows.
- Automation: integrate microbench into ci/perf harness. Record environment (GPU model, driver, CUDA, cuBLAS/cuDNN versions).

6) Practical implementation checklist (short-term priorities)
- [ ] Add FlashAttention thin wrapper with compatibility layer; unit tests for causal/non-causal and variable-length batches. (owner: Ravi)
- [ ] Implement QKV weight prepacking at model-load to support fused QKV GEMM (owner: Maya).
- [ ] Prototype device-side page table and small staging buffer for paged-KV; measure staging copy overhead vs indirection (owner: Diego).
- [ ] Implement async prefetch pipeline with separate transfer stream; add metrics (page transfer bytes/sec, prefetch queue length) (owner: Zoe).
- [ ] Autotune harness: collect kernel variant perf numbers and pick default heuristics (owner: Lena).

Open questions / risks
- How to keep behavioral determinism across fused kernels (especially for mixed-precision)? Need golden tests against reference kernels.
- Page-table size and update frequency: copying page table to device on every request may be expensive. Investigate delta-updates or persistent device-side page table that the host updates via atomic commands.
- Interplay with allocator: pinned staging buffers reduce system memory available. We need a global memory management policy.

References and notes
- FlashAttention paper & reference implementation.
- Our PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/342 (contains early benchmarks and microbench harness).
- Jira: JIRA-SRV-1287 (paged KV design spike).

Summary
- FlashAttention and operator fusion are high-impact wins for medium-to-long sequences and latency-sensitive small-batch requests.
- Paged KV enables large-context support for many concurrent requests but complexity centers on placement/eviction and transfer overlap.
- Prioritize a compatibility-first approach: add wrappers and fallbacks, collect perf telemetry, then enable aggressive fusion/paging heuristics per-model.

Notes to self:
- keep short-path for single-token decode minimal kernel walltime -> reduces p99.
- log when falling back from flashattention to reference kernel and add automated alert when fallback fraction > 5% on a node.
